post1.text:
Your exit valuation is decided years before you ever sit across from a buyer. Most founders don't realize this until it's too late.

A recent Entrepreneur.com piece made this point clearly: founders pour energy into growth but treat exit planning as something to handle later. Later is exactly when your options narrow and your leverage disappears.

Here's what leaders running $50M+ businesses need to understand:

1. Your multiple is not determined at the negotiating table. It's built through the quality of your revenue, your management depth, and your operational predictability over years, not months.

2. Strategic buyers and financial buyers value your company differently. Knowing which type of buyer you're building toward changes every decision you make today.

3. EBITDA adjustments are not just accounting cleanup. They are a direct lever on your final number, and most owners leave significant value on the table by not managing them proactively.

The companies that achieve premium multiples didn't get lucky. They built with the end in mind from the beginning.

What would you do differently in your business right now if you knew your exit was three years away?

post2.text:
A recent piece from J.P. Morgan Private Bank breaks down the core business exit strategies available to owners, from strategic sales and private equity recaps to family succession and IPOs.

It's a solid overview. But here's what it doesn't address: for companies in the $50M to $500M range, the exit strategy you choose has to be decided well before you're ready to execute it. That decision shapes how you structure your team, your financials, and your growth investments for years leading up to the event.

At Autobahn, we work with leaders who want to maximize their outcome, not just complete a transaction. Knowing your destination changes how you run the business today.

If you're scaling and haven't mapped your exit path yet, this article is a useful starting point.

post3.text:
A recent article on Entrepreneur.com captured something we hear from founders constantly: growth gets all the attention, and exit planning gets pushed to someday. Someday is a strategy that costs you millions.

Chapter 2 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, is titled "Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit" and was written by Paul Belair and George Hohman. They've been inside hundreds of transactions at the $50M to $500M scale, and they bring a level of specificity to this topic that most exit planning conversations never reach.

One thing they make clear early in the chapter: your multiple is not a reward for past performance. It's a reflection of how predictable your future performance looks to a buyer. That single reframe changes how you think about every operational decision you're making right now.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Most leadership teams don't fail at strategy. They fail at deciding what to stop doing.

Forbes recently broke down why execution collapses at the leadership level, and the pattern is consistent: too many priorities, unclear ownership, and no rhythm of accountability. The strategy isn't the problem. The operating system around it is.

If you're running a $50M+ business, here's what actually moves the needle:

1. Limit your annual priorities to five or fewer. Anything more is a wish list, not a plan.

2. Assign a single owner to each priority. Committees don't execute. People do.

3. Build a weekly cadence where leaders report progress in numbers, not status updates. Gut feelings don't scale.

The companies that grow from $50M to $500M aren't smarter. They're more disciplined about fewer things.

So here's the question worth sitting with: If your leadership team had to cut your current strategic priorities in half tomorrow, which ones would survive?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Forbes outlines exactly why leadership teams break down when it comes to executing strategy. The core issue: most companies treat strategy as an annual event rather than a daily operating discipline.

At Autobahn Consultants, we see this constantly with companies scaling through the $50M to $500M range. The strategy session happens, the slides look great, and then Q2 arrives and everyone is back to fighting fires.

The fix isn't a better planning template. It's building a leadership team that reviews, adjusts, and holds each other accountable on a weekly basis, not yearly.

If your strategy is gathering dust between offsite meetings, that's not a strategy problem. That's a leadership infrastructure problem.

Read the full Forbes piece here and tell us in the comments: how often does your leadership team formally review strategic progress?

post3.text:
The Forbes conversation around why leadership teams fail at execution hits close to home for us, because it's exactly the territory Rafa Loyo and Jim Randall cover in Chapter 3 of our upcoming book.

The chapter is called 'What We Learned Selling Fish Food and Nike Shoes,' and yes, it sounds unexpected. That's the point.

Rafa and Jim use two completely different businesses to reveal one consistent truth: the companies that scale don't have better strategies than their competitors. They have better systems for executing the ones they choose.

One insight they surface early: most growing companies are trying to win in too many directions at once, and that diffusion is invisible until it's expensive.

There's a framework in this chapter that will change how you run your next planning session. We'll leave it at that for now.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Most companies scaling past $50M already have a solid strategy. What they're missing is the operating discipline to execute it. Leadership teams confuse planning with progress, mistake activity for accountability, and wonder why the gap between their goals and their results keeps widening. The answer isn't a better strategy. It's a better system for running the one you already have.

post1.text:
Your brand is not your logo. It is not your tagline. It is the feeling people get when they interact with your company, and most CEOs at the $50M+ stage have never actually defined what that feeling should be.

Marketing Week recently reported that a fundamental lack of CEO understanding is actively undermining brand building in B2B companies. That tracks. When the person at the top treats brand as a marketing department problem, the whole organization pays for it in lost deals, higher churn, and price pressure.

Here is what scaling companies get wrong:

First, they confuse activity with strategy. Running campaigns is not the same as building a brand.

Second, brand consistency breaks down as headcount grows. New hires carry no institutional memory of what the company stands for.

Third, CEOs delegate brand entirely, then wonder why nothing feels cohesive.

Brand is a leadership responsibility before it is a marketing one. The CEO sets the standard, or nobody does.

So here is the question worth sitting with: If your best customer described your company to a stranger, what would they actually say?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Brand Innovators on JBL's marketing strategy makes a point that every scaling company should hear: JBL stopped organizing its marketing around campaigns and started organizing it around culture.

That is a significant shift. Campaigns have a start date and an end date. Culture does not.

For companies growing from $50M toward $500M, this distinction matters enormously. At that stage, you are adding people, entering new markets, and building new partnerships fast. If your brand only lives inside a campaign calendar, it collapses under that pressure.

The companies that scale well build a brand that employees can feel and repeat without a style guide in front of them. That is culture doing the work that campaigns cannot.

If you are leading a scaling organization and your brand lives in your marketing deck but not in your hallways, that is the problem worth solving first.

Read the full piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMikgFBVV95cUxPbXpYamE0dkF6MWVkcEkwUHlnSHk5bUtIbmV4ZTlDNEk3MEpURWZDdUo5b1Q4aTMtZkIzUy1scXU3VEJUREY2Vks0NjFGV0s2QXYtejBPMm93NlRrSC00MHRSdlpQcnJqeW00akp4eFRLeTZwRGxOV1BEQmR0eEpoVXB0cFpPaUhVeTBtU3E3WGxfZw

post3.text:
Marketing Week recently highlighted something we see constantly with scaling companies: CEOs are not close enough to brand strategy, and it is costing them growth.

Chapter 5 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, tackles this directly. The chapter is called 'What Does Your Marketing Smell Like?' and it was written by Kayli Simpson and Yasmin West, two practitioners who have seen brand misalignment stall companies that had every other advantage.

One of the sharpest ideas in the chapter is this: your brand communicates something whether you have defined it or not. The question is whether you are the one controlling that message or leaving it to chance.

For leaders scaling toward $500M, that is not a small distinction. Brand drift at scale is expensive and hard to reverse.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Most scaling companies have a marketing budget and no brand. They run campaigns, generate leads, and wonder why growth feels harder than it should. Here is the uncomfortable truth: by the time you hit $50M, your brand is already sending a signal. The only question is whether you built that signal on purpose or inherited it by accident.

post1.text:
Hiring more people is not a growth strategy. It is a budget problem waiting to happen.

SHRM's recent research on 2026 hiring trends makes this clear: the companies winning on talent are not casting the widest net. They are getting precise about who they need, why they need them, and what those people will actually produce.

For leaders scaling past $50M, this reframes the entire conversation. A few things worth sitting with:

First, headcount growth that outruns your management infrastructure creates chaos, not capacity. You need leaders in place before you need the bodies beneath them.

Second, your hiring criteria should be tied directly to the outcomes you need in the next 18 months, not the job descriptions you used three years ago.

Third, the cost of a wrong hire at this stage is not just financial. It is cultural, and culture repairs slowly.

Growth companies that treat talent acquisition as a volume exercise almost always stall before they hit the next threshold.

Where is your hiring process actually built for precision, and where is it just moving fast?

post2.text:
A recent piece in SHRM lays out what the best hiring teams already know heading into 2026: precision beats scale every time.

For companies in the $50M to $500M growth corridor, this is not a trend to monitor. It is an operational priority right now.

At Autobahn, we see it consistently. Scaling companies that define exactly what a role needs to produce before posting it fill seats faster, retain better, and align talent to revenue outcomes from day one. Companies that hire reactively, chasing headcount to keep pace with growth, spend the next 12 months managing the fallout.

If your hiring process was built when you were half your current size, it is overdue for a hard look.

Read the full SHRM piece here and then ask yourself whether your talent acquisition strategy is built for the company you are today or the one you were.

post3.text:
The conversation around precision hiring is not new to us. It sits at the core of Chapter 6 in our upcoming book, Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond.

Chapter 6, The Talent Engine, was written by Caleb Hawkins, Darla Klein, and Yasmin West. Together they work with scaling companies every day, and what they have found is that talent problems at this stage are rarely about finding enough people. They are about building the infrastructure to identify, place, and develop the right people before growth demands force bad decisions.

One idea from the chapter worth sitting with: the leaders who scale successfully do not just hire for today's open seat. They hire with a picture of the organization they are building 36 months out.

There is a framework behind that thinking, and it changes how leadership teams approach every hire they make.

Rock Your Business: available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
More KPIs will not fix your business. They will bury it.

Most leadership teams at the $50M+ level are not suffering from a lack of data. They are drowning in it. Oracle NetSuite recently published a list of 30 financial metrics companies should track heading into 2026. Thirty. If your team is reviewing that many numbers in a single meeting, you are not managing performance. You are managing a spreadsheet.

Here is what actually works for scaling companies:

First, ruthless prioritization. Your leadership team should own no more than 5 to 7 KPIs at any given time. If everything is a priority, nothing is.

Second, lag versus lead distinction. Most companies track outcomes. The ones that scale fast track the leading indicators that predict those outcomes weeks in advance.

Third, accountability with teeth. A KPI without a named owner and a defined consequence is just a number on a slide.

The companies that move from $50M to $500M do not track more. They track better.

How many KPIs does your leadership team actually review every week?

post2.text:
A recent piece from CliftonLarsonAllen breaks down the KPIs manufacturers should be using to improve company performance. It is a solid framework for the shop floor level.

But here is what the article does not address: what happens when a manufacturing company hits $50M and the metrics that got them there start working against them.

At that stage, the problem is rarely a missing KPI. It is that leadership is still running on the same five numbers they used when the business was $10M. The complexity has multiplied. The dashboard has not.

Scaling companies need metrics that stretch up and down the org. Operational data has to connect to financial outcomes, and both have to connect to the people accountable for moving them.

If your metrics are not driving decisions, they are just decoration.

Read the full CLA piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiugFBVV95cUxNc3hGVVVxVnMwVEpLcmxaNWJzaURJbERjczZaSDhlcnhvOFlHX1VZU0tETkctQjFqRVhZVkNtcFNoUWtfSmRhSmU5N3pYc25IVzlfTEs5TjFZWk1RTmhZd2JzSkpPSXVmQndRRHRBM29CaDBoWnVWRXcxMnBhWkcwT3dmWTAwSDFSeS1hYzFtRUNtd05nWE9PX25nbzRfc2ZzSjVFVURMY0hMRkdVMmtOdjVOYUluUXJIcEE

post3.text:
There is a reason Chapter 7 of our upcoming book is called "Death by KPIs."

Authors Hector Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall have worked with enough scaling companies to know that the metric problem is not a data problem. It is a discipline problem. Leaders add KPIs when things go wrong. They rarely subtract them when things stabilize. Over time, the dashboard becomes noise, and the team stops trusting the numbers at all.

Chapter 7 introduces a clear way to think about which metrics belong at which level of your organization, and how to build accountability structures that make those numbers mean something.

One thing it will challenge you on: the KPI your leadership team fights to keep on the list is often the one that needs to go.

Rock Your Business, by Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, available soon. Follow us for updates.

The leadership team is reviewing 20 metrics, owning none of them, and wondering why nothing changes quarter over quarter. The path from $50M to $500M runs directly through the uncomfortable work of cutting your KPIs in half and holding someone accountable for each one that remains.

post1.text:
AI is making executives more productive while leaving their businesses behind. That is not a paradox. It is a warning.

A recent Fortune report found that 90% of executives say AI has not moved the needle on company-wide productivity. Yet the same leaders are cutting headcount based on AI's promise. That is a dangerous gap between personal efficiency and organizational results.

Here is what scaling companies need to understand:

1. Individual productivity gains do not automatically become company-wide gains. You need systems, not just tools.

2. AI adoption without process redesign is just expensive automation of the same broken workflows.

3. The leaders winning with AI are not the ones using it most. They are the ones deploying it most intentionally, at the right points in the value chain.

If you run a $50M to $500M business, the question is not whether your team uses AI. It is whether AI is actually wired into how your company creates and delivers value.

So where in your business is AI genuinely moving outcomes, not just saving time on emails?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fortune stopped us cold: 90% of executives report that AI has not improved productivity at the business level, yet layoffs tied to AI expectations are already happening.

For companies in the $50M to $500M range, this is a critical signal. At this stage of growth, every structural decision compounds. If you are cutting people based on AI productivity gains that have not materialized organizationally, you are betting the business on an assumption, not a result.

At Autobahn, we work with leaders who are scaling fast. The ones navigating AI well are treating it as an operational design problem, not a technology problem.

Before your next AI-related headcount or investment decision, ask your team: where is the proof of value at the system level, not just the individual level?

post1.text:
The most dangerous leaders in a scaling company are the ones who stopped feeling like impostors.

Imposter syndrome gets treated as a problem to fix. It is not. At the $50M to $500M growth stage, the leaders causing the most damage are the ones with absolute certainty and zero self-questioning. The ones quietly doubting themselves are often the ones still learning.

Forbes Australia recently reported that imposter syndrome tends to follow high achievers straight to the top. That finding should reframe how growth-stage executives think about self-doubt entirely.

Three things worth sitting with:

1. Self-doubt, when managed, sharpens your judgment. Overconfidence at scale is how blind spots become catastrophic.

2. The feeling that you do not fully belong in the room often means you are in exactly the right room.

3. Leaders who acknowledge uncertainty build teams that flag real problems. Leaders who perform certainty build teams that hide them.

Your company cannot outgrow the psychology of the person running it.

So here is the question: Is your self-doubt making you a better leader, or are you just running from it?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Bona Magazine explored how leaders can reframe imposter syndrome not as a liability but as a foundation for genuine executive presence.

That framing matters a lot for companies scaling past $50M.

At that stage, the leadership identity issues that were manageable at $10M become organizational problems. When a CEO privately believes they got lucky, they underhire, avoid bold decisions, and build cultures that mirror their own self-doubt.

At Autobahn Consultants, we see this pattern consistently. The internal narrative of the person at the top shapes every system, team, and strategy below them.

The goal is not to eliminate the doubt. It is to stop letting it make decisions for you.

Read the full piece and consider where your own leadership psychology might be quietly setting the ceiling for your company's growth.

The title is not rhetorical. It is the exact question scaling leaders need to ask themselves.

Coauthored by Samantha Frost, Caleb Hawkins, and Rafa Loyo, this chapter tackles something most business books skip entirely: the psychology of the person driving growth. Specifically, how imposter syndrome does not disappear as your company gets bigger. It just gets more expensive.

One of the sharper insights in this chapter is that the feelings of fraudulence scaling leaders experience are often a signal worth decoding, not a weakness to suppress. What you do with that signal determines whether you grow into the role or quietly shrink from it.

post1.text:
The most dangerous blind spot for leaders running $50M+ companies is not a bad strategy. It is a life they never actually designed.

Most executives can tell you their five-year revenue target down to the decimal. Ask them what they want their life to look like when they get there, and you get silence.

A recent Entrepreneur piece made this plain: founders obsess over growth plans but rarely build an exit plan, and even fewer build a life plan to follow it. The business gets a roadmap. The person running it does not.

Here is what that costs you at scale:

First, you optimize for the business at the expense of your health, relationships, and identity without ever making a conscious choice to do so.

Second, when a liquidity event or leadership transition finally arrives, you have no idea who you are outside the company.

Third, your best people watch you burn out and quietly update their resumes.

Growth without intentional life design is just a faster route to the wrong destination.

What would you change about your life if the revenue target were already hit?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fortune, published alongside research from Morgan Stanley, lays out what entrepreneurs actually face after selling a business. The financial complexity is real. But the harder part is the identity vacuum that follows.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern well before an exit. Leaders scaling from $50M toward $500M often defer every personal decision until after the next milestone. That deferral becomes a habit, and the habit becomes a trap.

If you are building a company at scale, the time to design your life is not after the transaction. It is now, while you still have the leverage and the clarity to make deliberate choices.

Read the Fortune piece here and then ask yourself whether your personal roadmap is getting the same attention as your business plan.

Scaling a company to $500M is hard. Knowing what you actually want when you get there is harder.

Chapter 10 of Rock Your Business, titled Coming Up for Air, tackles this head-on. Written by Samantha Frost alongside Jonathan and Katherine Slain, the chapter is built for leaders who have been so locked into growth mode that they have never stopped to design the life running alongside the business.

One insight from the chapter that stays with you: the leaders who thrive at scale are not the ones who sacrifice everything for the company. They are the ones who get intentional about what they are building toward, personally, before the pressure makes that choice for them.

There is a framework inside that changes how you think about the relationship between your business goals and your life goals. We will leave the details for the pages.
